concepts.name: The Three Sangams (Muthal Sangam, Idai Sangam, Kadai Sangam): Historicity and Legend
key_dimensions: Legendary vs. historical evidence for each Sangam's existence and location (Madurai, Kapadapuram, etc.)
Duration and number of poets associated with each Sangam as per tradition
Role of Pandya kings as patrons and the submergence of early Sangam cities (lost land of Kumari Kandam)
UPSC trap: Only the Third Sangam has substantial surviving literary evidence — distinguishing myth from history

concepts.name: Eightfold Anthologies (Ettuthokai): Composition and Classification
key_dimensions: Names of all eight anthologies: Ainkurunuru, Akananuru, Purananuru, Kuruntokai, Kalittokai, Natrinai, Paripatal, Pathitrupattu
Classification into Akam (love/interior) and Puram (heroic/exterior) poetry
Distinguishing features: meter, length, thematic focus of each anthology
UPSC trap: Kalittokai and Paripatal are sometimes considered transitional — not purely Akam or Puram

concepts.name: Ten Idylls (Pathupattu): Poems and Their Significance
key_dimensions: Names of all ten idylls: Thirumurugatrupadai, Porunararrupadai, Sirupananatrupadai, Perumpanatrupadai, Mullaippattu, Maduraikkanji, Nedunalatai, Kurinjippattu, Pattinappalai, Malaipatukatam
Nature as 'Guide poems' (Aatrupadai) — poets directing other poets to royal patrons
Maduraikkanji as a unique source for Sangam-era economy, trade, and urban life
UPSC trap: Not all ten are Aatrupadai type — distinguishing guide poems from descriptive poems

concepts.name: Akam (Interior) Poetry: The Tinai System of Five Landscapes
key_dimensions: Five Tinais: Kurinji (mountains/union), Mullai (forests/patient waiting), Marutam (pastoral/infidelity), Neytal (coastal/separation/longing), Palai (wasteland/separation/journey)
Each Tinai's associated flower, bird, time of day, season, and emotional theme (Kaikkilai and Perundinam as the two marginal tinais)
Structural formula: landscape as objective correlative for emotional states
UPSC trap: Palai is not a fixed landscape but a transformed, harsh version — often confused as a sixth landscape

concepts.name: Puram (Exterior) Poetry: Themes of Heroism, Death, and Patronage
key_dimensions: Sub-genres: Vetchi (cattle raid), Vaakai (victory), Kanji (transience of life), Potini (siege), Ulinai (battle)
The concept of 'Maranam' (heroic death) and 'Nadugal' (memorial stones) as evidenced in Purananuru
Role of women (mothers, wives) celebrating rather than mourning heroic death — unique cultural dimension
Purananuru as a primary historical source for Sangam-era polity and society

concepts.name: Thirukkural by Thiruvalluvar: Structure, Philosophy, and Universal Appeal
key_dimensions: Three-part structure: Aram (virtue/dharma), Porul (wealth/polity), Inbam (love/pleasure) — 133 chapters, 1330 couplets
Secular and non-sectarian philosophy — absence of explicit religious affiliation debated by scholars
Influence on Tamil identity, UNESCO recognition, and translations into over 80 languages
UPSC trap: Thirukkural is classified as part of the 'Eighteen Minor Works' (Pathinenkilkanakku), NOT the Ettuthokai or Pathupattu

concepts.name: Silappatikaram by Ilango Adigal: Epic Narrative and Socio-Political Commentary
key_dimensions: Story of Kovalan, Kannagi, and Madhavi — themes of justice, chastity (Karpu), and royal wrongdoing
Author Ilango Adigal identified as a Jain/Buddhist prince — debate on religious affiliation
Multi-kingdom setting (Chera, Chola, Pandya) as a source for Sangam-era political geography
Silappatikaram as the first Tamil epic (Mupperum Kaviyam) — significance of Kannagi as a cultural icon

concepts.name: Manimekalai by Sattanar: Buddhist Philosophy in Epic Form
key_dimensions: Sequel to Silappatikaram — story of Manimekalai, daughter of Kovalan and Madhavi, embracing Buddhism
Propagation of Mahayana Buddhism and compassion (Karuna) as central themes
Contrast with Silappatikaram: Jain/Hindu influences vs. Buddhist philosophy
UPSC trap: Manimekalai is explicitly Buddhist while Silappatikaram's religious affiliation is debated — common confusion

concepts.name: Sangam-Era Social Structure: Caste, Gender, and Community as Reflected in Literature
key_dimensions: Relatively fluid social structure — evidence of inter-caste interaction and women poets (Avvaiyar, Nakkirar)
Women poets in Sangam literature: Avvaiyar, Kakkaipadiniyar, Uraiyur Muthukooththan — their contributions
Devadasi system, bards (Panar), and the role of professional poet-patrons relationship
UPSC trap: 'Avvaiyar' is not one poet but refers to multiple poets across different periods — Sangam Avvaiyar vs. later Avvaiyar

concepts.name: Sangam-Era Polity: Three Crowned Kings (Muvendhar) and Their Portrayal
key_dimensions: Cheras (capital Vanji/Karur), Cholas (capital Uraiyur/Puhar), Pandyas (capital Madurai) — distinct emblems and symbols
Pathitrupattu as the primary source for Chera kings; Purananuru for all three dynasties
Concept of 'Irai' (tribute) and 'Kadai' (gift-giving) — patron-poet economic relationship
Battle of Venni (Chola victory) and Battle of Talaikottam — historically significant events in Sangam poetry

concepts.name: Tolkappiyam by Tolkappiyar: Grammar, Poetics, and Its Foundational Status
key_dimensions: Oldest surviving Tamil grammar text — three books: Ezhuttatikaram (phonology), Sollatikaram (morphology), Porulatikaram (poetics/semantics)
Porulatikaram codifies the Tinai system — Tolkappiyam as the theoretical framework for Sangam poetry
Debate on Tolkappiyam's dating: pre-Sangam, early Sangam, or post-Sangam composition
UPSC trap: Tolkappiyam is NOT part of Ettuthokai or Pathupattu — it is a grammatical treatise, foundational but separate

concepts.name: Trade, Economy, and Urban Life in Sangam Literature: Archaeological Corroboration
key_dimensions: Puhar (Kaveripattinam) as a major port — described in Pattinappalai and Silappatikaram; corroborated by archaeology
References to Roman trade (Yavanas/Greeks) in Akananuru, Purananuru — wine, lamps, gold coins
Pepper, pearls, ivory, and muslin as key exports — Sangam literature as a trade history source
Correlation with Periplus of the Erythraean Sea and Pliny's Natural History for external validation

concepts.name: Religion and Philosophy in Sangam Literature: Pluralism and Early Bhakti Roots
key_dimensions: Presence of Vedic, Jain, Buddhist, and folk religious elements — absence of rigid sectarianism
Muruga worship (Thirumurugatrupadai) as earliest evidence of Tamil Shaivism and proto-Bhakti
Paripatal as the anthology most explicitly devotional — dedicated to Vishnu and Murugan
Sangam literature as precursor to later Bhakti movement (Nayanmars and Alvars) — continuity vs. rupture debate

concepts.name: Concept of 'Aram' (Dharma/Ethics) in Sangam and Post-Sangam Tamil Literature
key_dimensions: Aram as social ethics — differentiated from Vedic Dharma; rooted in Tamil moral philosophy
Thirukkural's Arattuppal as the definitive treatment; echoed in Naladiyar and Pazhamozhi Nanuru
Distinction between personal virtue (Aram), political economy (Porul), and love (Inbam) as a unique tripartite framework
UPSC trap: The Thirukkural's ethical framework is often compared to Arthashastra — key difference: Kural's ethics are non-authoritarian and universal

concepts.name: The Eighteen Minor Works (Pathinenkilkanakku): Didactic Literature
key_dimensions: Collection of 18 didactic texts including Thirukkural, Naladiyar, Pazhamozhi Nanuru, Inna Narpathu
Naladiyar — Jain authorship, 400 quatrains on ethics, often compared to Thirukkural
Transition from Sangam secular poetry to moralistic/didactic literature — historical-cultural shift
UPSC trap: Pathinenkilkanakku ('eighteen lower/minor works') is distinct from Ettuthokai and Pathupattu — 'lower' refers to shorter verse form, not lower importance

concepts.name: Sangam Literature as Historical Source: Methodology and Limitations
key_dimensions: Evidence for: social customs, trade routes, political history, geography, flora and fauna
Limitations: poetic exaggeration (Uvama/simile conventions), patronage bias, oral transmission distortions
U.V. Swaminatha Iyer's role in rediscovering and editing Sangam manuscripts in the 19th–20th century
Comparison with Arthashastra and Ashokan edicts as historical sources — Sangam literature's unique cultural-literary lens

concepts.name: Cilappatikaram's Kannagi: Symbol of Justice, Womanhood, and Tamil Nationalism
key_dimensions: Narrative: Kannagi's curse destroying Madurai after unjust execution of Kovalan by Pandya king
Theological dimension: Kannagi deified as 'Pattini' goddess — worship spread to Sri Lanka and Southeast Asia
Modern resonance: Kannagi statue as a symbol of Tamil women's rights and anti-oppression movements
UPSC trap: Pattini cult spread to Sri Lanka (Sinhalese tradition) — demonstrating Sangam literature's transnational cultural impact

concepts.name: Aatrupadai (Guide Poems): Genre Characteristics and Economic Significance
key_dimensions: Genre convention: a successful poet guides a poor poet to a generous royal patron, describing the journey and patron's generosity
Six Aatrupadai texts within Pathupattu: Thirumurugatrupadai, Porunararrupadai, Sirupananatrupadai, Perumpanatrupadai, Pattinappalai, Malaipatukatam
Economic model of literary patronage: gifts of gold, elephants, chariots — evidence for Sangam gift economy
UPSC trap: Not all ten Pathupattu poems are Aatrupadai — Mullaippattu, Kurinjippattu, Maduraikkanji, Nedunalatai are NOT guide poems

concepts.name: Sangam Literature's Influence on Later Tamil Cultural Traditions: Continuity and Transformation
key_dimensions: Bhakti movement (6th–9th century CE): Nayanmars' Tevaram and Alvars' Divya Prabandham drawing on Sangam poetic conventions
Tinai system's influence on classical Carnatic music raga-emotion (rasa) associations
Revival of Sangam literature in Tamil nationalism (19th–20th century): U.V. Swaminatha Iyer, Maraimalai Adigal, Dravidian politics
UNESCO and global recognition — Tamil as a Classical Language (2004) largely argued through Sangam literature's antiquity
